passage:
Devika, sit with me. Your Nani, Manjula, wasn't always the person making you tea.

At twenty I was with a boy called Dinesh. One day he said I'd been flirting with a boy at the bus queue. I hadn't; he'd only asked which bus went to the market. I told him so, calmly. He grumbled, then let it go.

Two weeks later it was a classmate's notes. Then a smile at the shop. Every time I explained, and every time a new accusation came, as if my answers were never the point.

I began to wonder if I'd done something wrong. Then I stopped and looked at the pattern instead. Nothing I said ever ended it.

I told my sister everything. That's what helped me see that the problem was not my behaviour.

qa.q: Why had Dinesh said Manjula was flirting at the bus queue?
qa.a: He accused her because a boy in the queue had spoken to her, though he had only asked which bus went to the market.

qa.q: How did Manjula feel as new accusations kept coming, and what changed?
qa.a: She began to feel confused and full of self-doubt, wondering if she had done something wrong, until she saw that nothing she said ever ended the accusations, so the problem was the pattern and not her behaviour.

qa.q: What helped Manjula see her situation more clearly?
qa.a: Telling her sister everything, because a trusted listener helped her see the pattern from outside.

qa.q: How might Dinesh have seen his own accusations at the time?
qa.a: He may have felt insecure and believed he was being watchful, without seeing that his suspicion had no end.

grounding: Shows being accused of things not done, answering calmly with facts, and recognising constant unfounded suspicion as a warning sign.
